newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Fipe deflation at 0.03 pct in Nov 8-Dec 8.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Fipe deflation at 0.03 pct in Nov 8-Dec 8.

text.p: Brazil's consumer prices fell 0.03 percent in the Nov 8-Dec 8 period, the first time since June 1957 that the country has registered deflation, an official at the Economic Research Institute (Fipe) said.
"It's great and the trend is likely to continue," said Juarez Rizzieri, the president of Fipe.
Prices fell in the period, compared with 0.34 percent inflation in the prior four-week period, due mostly to a drop in food prices, he added.
A slight decline in personal expenses also contributed to the decline in the index, which measures prices in the Sao Paulo area, Rizzieri said.
The declining prices offset hikes in housing, education and health costs, he said.
"Brazil has not seen this since the days of Juscelino," he said, referring to Juscelino Kubitschek, who was Brazil's president in the late 1950s.
"But it's totally different. Th 1950s was a period of great economic expansion as well as low inflation. Today, we have low inflation but also weak growth."

Rizzieri estimated December could end with close to zero inflation or slight deflation, versus November's 0.34-percent rise, due to declining food prices and slower-than-expected sales this Christmas season.
"It could be zero or remain negative," he said. "Food prices is one of reasons, but we may also see retailers holding sales to get rid of high stocks."
Brazilians this year are more apt to use their 13th monthly wage to pay debts rather than go on pre-Christmas shopping sprees, he added.
Rizzieri released the following breakdown of the weighted Fipe inflation index for the four-week period ended Dec 8:
-Food: -0.60 pct fall in the period
-Housing: 0.51 pct rise in the period
-Transportation: 0.04 pct rise in the period
-Personal expenses: -0.03 pct fall in the period
-Clothing: 0.07 pct rise in the period
-Health care: 0.13 pct rise in the period
-Education: 0.29 pct rise in the period
The Fipe index is calculated by the University of Sao Paulo, which releases inflation figures at weekly intervals.
--James Craig, Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248-5413
